name: Lubukusu
confidence_why: Ng'ang'a (2008) is the only first-hand account that states stress at all, placing it on the lengthened penultimate syllable of Lubukusu nouns and verbs, which fits Hubbard's (1994) measured extra penultimate duration, but Downing (2005) lists Bukusu among Bantu languages with no reported stress and Mutonyi (1992, 1996) describes the prosody without mentioning stress, so the penultimate reading rests on a single asserted, unmeasured statement.

catalog_quote: p.97, sec. 4.2.1 Tone as a Marker of Syllable Prominence: "The penultimate syllable is made to stand out clearly when nouns and verbs are articulated. The penultimate syllable is mostly lengthened; therefore it is hospitable to contour tones. The penultimate syllable carry word stress, therefore contour tones add to its prominence as shown in example 4.1.3 above. This is also illustrated in example below Verbs HL a#kone:l-e (he slept on/on behalf of) HL a#meke:l-e (he cut for/on behalf of)" | p.72: "Zhang, (2001) observes that contours occur in stressed stem positions and the stressed stem position is the penultimate syllable in verbs and nouns. ... This section shows that H tones and HL/LH contour tones occur on the penultimate syllable of the noun stems and verb stems." | p.119, Tone Anticipation as a Sign of Strength (SOS): "/H/ tone is anticipated to the penultimate syllable of the verb stems because it is a position where stress falls (as in 4.1.3 above)." | p.120: "The metrically strong position or the accented position is the most prominent position." | p.131 (conclusion): "Even though tones are affected by the domain edges, stress placement plays a role in the assignment of the /HL/, /LH/ and /H/ tones to the penultimate and word final positions in nouns and verbs in Lubukusu. In addition the syllable length in nouns and verbs determine the tone assigned."
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Bukusu (buku1249) is not in the catalog. Both title-hit items are non-yielding for word stress. Mutonyi 1992 (OSU WPL 41, open on the OSU Knowledge Bank, already held by the project and re-read) is about moraic structure and compensatory lengthening; it contains no stress/accent statement at all. Philippson's 1991/1992 Paris 5 Thèse d'État on tone and accent in East African Bantu is print/microfiche only (theses.fr 'accessible: non'; SUDOC holdings at Paris-UPCité, CTLES, Montpellier, Strasbourg BNU, Paris BIS; not on HAL); its abstract describes a ~30-language continuum from pure tone (Kikuyu) to demarcative penultimate accent (Swahili) without naming Bukusu, and the open 1998 Faits de langues derivative (downloaded from Persée, saved as per-page text) never mentions Bukusu or Luyia. No first-hand statement of Bukusu word stress was read in this search of works with stress in the title; the only bearing on the question remains the second-hand Google Books snippet already logged by the earlier reading (Downing 2005b: Gikuyu and Bukusu 'have no reported stress'; Hubbard 1994: penultimate syllable receives extra duration), which was not opened as full text. Priority for acquisition: Philippson thesis medium (survey may include Bukusu but the abstract does not show it); the better targets for a first-hand Bukusu prosody statement remain de Blois 1975 (RMCA, print), Austen 1974 (SAL Suppl. 5) and Mutonyi 2000 (OSU PhD, ProQuest) from the earlier reading. All downloaded records are and logged in there.

new_statements.quote: Mutonyi 1996:77-78: "Bukusu, which has preserved the Proto-Bantu H(igh)/Low lexical tone contrast in its verbs, displays classic tense-determined tone alternations ... it will be shown that there are at least three kinds of H tones involved. These include two lexical H tones, which are the stem H and object prefix H tones, a tense-aspect imposed melodic H, and a phrasal H tone inserted between any two adjacent words." Downing 2005b (snippet): "... continuum of stress systems, from languages like Swahili (G42) which have uncontroversial word stress, to languages like Gikuyu (E51) and Bukusu (J31c), which have no reported stress, to the Southern Bantu languages illustrated in (2) and (3) above, which lie somewhere in between these two extremes."

new_statements.rule_in_words: Bukusu is described first-hand only as a tone language (privative H vs toneless roots, melodic and phrasal H tones, mora as TBU); no accessible primary description states a word-stress or accent position, and Downing (2005b), who did fieldwork-based work on Bukusu reduplication, characterises Bukusu as a language with 'no reported stress'. Hubbard 1994 (snippet only) reports extra phonetic duration on the penultimate syllable in her Bukusu measurements, i.e. possible phrase-level penultimate lengthening, unverified.
new_statements.exceptions: none; Mutonyi 1996:109 notes a prepausal H retracts or deletes depending on penult length (tonal, not stress).
new_statements.domain_note: Tone statements concern verbs in isolation and in phrases (phrasal H between words). The 'no reported stress' remark is a typological aside in a survey-style chapter, not a dedicated prosodic description; the deciding primary works (Mutonyi 2000, de Blois 1975, Austen 1974a/b) could not be opened.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe Bukusu/Lubukusu (JE31c, buku1249) of Bungoma, western Kenya; Mutonyi's data are his own (native speaker) dialect. Hubbard's and Downing's Bukusu data also derive from work with Mutonyi. No dialect mismatch; Tachoni and Gisu/Masaaba are separate glottocodes and were not used.

Also compatible with the existing Mutonyi 1996 tone statement (tone language with a stress statement). Confirmed verbatim against the p.97 page scan.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Lubukusu is a two-tone (H/L) register tone language (p.2); the penultimate syllable of nouns and verbs carries word stress, is lengthened, and is the position that attracts contour tones and anticipated H tones.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated; p.135 says the role of length and stress in tone realisation 'requires further investigation'. The penult-stress claim is asserted (partly via Zhang 2001) rather than argued from phonetic measurement.
new_statements.identity_note: Ng'ang'a 2008 describes Lubukusu as spoken in Kibingei location, Bungoma district, Western Kenya (two informants, plus the author as native speaker), chosen because it does not border other Luyia dialects (Tachoni, Kabras, Nyala, Wanga). Safir & Sikuku 2011 is Lubukusu without dialect specification. Philippson 1992 is a comparative East African Bantu thesis; its abstract names only Kikuyu and Swahili.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog codes Lubukusu as fixed penultimate stress (Ng'ang'a 2008 p.97: penult lengthened, carries word stress, hosts contours). Philippson, summarising the 1970s tonological descriptions, explicitly puts Bukusu among the languages where the penultimate 'plays no role whatsoever' and enters 'néant' under 'status of the penultimate syllable', treating its 'accent' as a lexical tonal (pitch accent-type) mark, not a positional stress. It agrees with the existing statements that Bukusu is tonal with lexical H contrasts and contrastive vowel length, but differs from the catalog on the type and existence of penultimate prominence.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Philippson analyses Bukusu (E31a, data from De Blois 1975 and Austen 1974) as an 'accentual' tone system: lexically marked moras (a diacritic accent) receive a *L-H melody, the H surfacing on the mora after the marked one, with post-lexical phrasal H insertion and pre-pausal delinking of the last H; surface vowel length is contrastive; and, unlike Nande (penult = 'culmination d'intensité et de longueur') or Sukuma (demarcative penult accent), the penultimate syllable has NO special status in Bukusu ('néant'; 'la pénultième ne semble jouer aucun rôle, quel qu'il soit'). No stress placement rule is given because none is recognised.
new_statements.exceptions: A special rule puts the H on the augment itself when it is group-initial (p.336 n.2); (…B)BH noun stems surface (…B)BB before most possessives/demonstratives (3.4.1); Meeussen's rule applies only stem-internally (p.462). None concern stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Philippson's 'bukusu' = Guthrie E31a, groupe VII (Luhya), graded '++' (well described) in his Tableau 1, sources Austen 1974 and De Blois 1975 (Kimilili-area Bukusu); Mutonyi 2000 describes Bukusu (Lubukusu) of Bungoma District, western Kenya (author a native speaker; same variety as his 1992/1996 OSU WPL papers held by the project). Both are the catalog language Lubukusu, glottocode buku1249, ISO bxk.

tone_statements.quote: Nouns belong to one of many tonal classes; two are parallel to the verb tone classes … Some nouns are all L, others realize a H just on a prefix … Verbs belong to one of two tonal classes: H-toned or toneless verbs … In contexts with no tonal melody: Ø verbs are all low, H verbs are H on a prefix … Tone plays a role in marking TAMP distinctions … In the Indefinite Future, “melodic Hs” target μ1 in Ø verbs, μ1 of σ2 in H verbs

tone_statements.summary: Privative lexical contrast of /H/ vs toneless roots in nouns and verbs; toneless words surface all low; melodic H tones mark tense-aspect, docking on set moras; plateau, H spread, downstep in phrases.

readall_conflicts: A standing tension from earlier passes remains: Downing 2005b (Google Books snippet, second-hand) lists Bukusu among languages 'which have no reported stress', whereas Ng'ang'a 2008 asserts penultimate word stress (with penultimate lengthening) explicitly; Ng'ang'a's claim is asserted, partly via Zhang 2001, without acoustic evidence, and the thesis itself says (p.135) that the role of length and stress in tone realisation 'requires further investigation'. Mutonyi 2000, Philippson 1992 and Scruggs 1980 could not be opened. Philippson 1991 (read, pp.485, 497/502, 336-338), working from De Blois 1975 and Austen 1974, classifies Bukusu as a lexical tonal-accent ('système accentuel', *L-H melody on marked moras) language with contrastive vowel length in which the penultimate syllable has no special status at all ('néant'; 'la pénultième ne semble jouer aucun rôle, quel qu'il soit'), whereas the catalog record (Ng'ang'a 2008 MA, p.97, page scan checked) states that the penultimate syllable is lengthened and carries word stress, coded as fixed penultimate stress. The two agree that Lubukusu is a tone language with lexical H contrasts (as do Mutonyi 1992/1996 held by the project); they disagree on whether there is penultimate stress/prominence. Mutonyi 2000, the fullest modern phonology (advisor Odden; Otundo 2018 cites its p.145 on vowel length), could not be obtained to settle: it exists only behind ProQuest (docview 304634265, UMI 9994910) and in print/microfiche at OSU. sources.quote: Ces systèmes varient en effet depuis des langues pleinement tonales (kikuyu) jusqu'à des langues à accent démarcatif pénultième (swahili), tous les cas intermédiaires étant représentés. ... Une trentaine de langues en tout sont utilisées comme exemples. Enfin, on établit systématiquement les correspondances prosodiques entre chacune des langues concernées et le bantu commun et on propose l'hypothèse que le moteur principal de l'évolution des systèmes concernés a été l'émergence d'un accent démarcatif sur la pénultième servant de limite de domaine pour l'association tonale. [tr.: These systems range from fully tonal languages (Kikuyu) to languages with demarcative penultimate accent (Swahili), with every intermediate case represented. ... Some thirty languages in all are used as examples. Finally ... the hypothesis is proposed that the main driver of the evolution of these systems was the emergence of a demarcative accent on the penult serving as a domain limit for tone association.]

sources.quote: Our task in this paper is not to try and resolve the dilemma faced by phonologists in this regard, but rather to examine a few prosodic structures in Bukusu which seem to favor the moraic theory over CV phonology. ... In section 3, I adduce evidence for the four processes which trigger compensatory lengthening (CL)
sources.note: Nothing. 'Prosodic structure' in the title means moraic/skeletal structure: the paper treats compensatory lengthening from glide formation, vowel contraction, pre-nasal-consonant lengthening and prefix haplology, and touches tone only incidentally (fn. on H placement on stem moras, falling tone on lengthened preprefix vowels). The strings 'stress', 'accent', 'penult' and 'prominen' do not occur anywhere in the text.

sources.citation: [Ebarb, Kristopher J. & Michael R. Marlo, per search-engine summary - not verified on the record]. n.d. [Poster] Tone assignment in Bukusu nouns and verbs. Conference poster, Academia.edu document 26961616.
sources.quote: Nouns belong to one of many tonal classes; two are parallel to the verb tone classes … Some nouns are all L, others realize a H just on a prefix … Verbs belong to one of two tonal classes: H-toned or toneless verbs … In contexts with no tonal melody: Ø verbs are all low, H verbs are H on a prefix … Tone plays a role in marking TAMP distinctions … In the Indefinite Future, “melodic Hs” target μ1 in Ø verbs, μ1 of σ2 in H verbs
sources.locator: 1-page poster, box 1 'General Tonal Properties' and box 'Positions targeted within the stem'; also 'Ø vs. H roots' l.117, 'Ø vs. H in monosyllabic nouns' l.114
sources.note: Privative lexical contrast of /H/ vs toneless roots in nouns and verbs; toneless words surface all low; melodic H tones mark tense-aspect, docking on set moras; plateau, H spread, downstep in phrases.
